evidence.text: A declaration establishes a political statement; other records are needed for the lives of its many participants.

name: Haiti: freedom fought for in a plantation world
geographicPrecision: Gonaïves declaration-region locator; the revolution involved many places and changing alliances.

interval.label: Revolutionary investigation, 1791–1804
interval.note: Uprising to independence; not the end of the consequences of slavery or colonial power.

question: Who made freedom, and why was it contested?
summary: Enslaved people’s resistance broke the plantation order, but emancipation, control of work and independence were distinct struggles. Regional research, a leader’s letter and constitutional rules show people making different political choices. The 1804 declaration severed French rule while also establishing authority; it does not speak directly for every household.

sections.title: Resistance grew through different local struggles
sections.text: Sugar and coffee production depended on coerced work. In 1791, enslaved people challenged that order in the northern plantation region. Sabine Manigat’s research distinguishes this uprising from different conflicts in the West and South. Insurgent groups, free people of color, colonists and competing armies formed shifting alliances rather than one stable camp. War and negotiation created openings for people seeking liberty. Regional differences help explain how a struggle could change direction without assuming everyone began with the same plan for an independent nation.

sections.title: Emancipation had to be defended and interpreted
sections.text: Provincial emancipation measures in 1793 preceded the French Convention’s 1794 colonial abolition decree. Deputies carried events in Saint-Domingue into metropolitan politics. Louverture, a formerly enslaved leader, offers one particular political voice. His 1797 letter asks Vincent to defend him before the Directory, rejects racist accusations and affirms attachment to France. The argument makes sense within that moment’s commitments. It does not turn him into the spokesman for every cultivator, nor make independence the inevitable meaning of all earlier resistance.

citations.locator: Le débat: provincial measures, delegation and decree

sections.title: Ending slavery did not settle control of work
sections.text: The 1801 constitution prohibits slavery and calls people free and French. It also insists that cultivation continue. Articles 15–16 picture an estate as a family led by its owner or representative, promise cultivators a share of revenues and treat changes of residence as a threat to production. The governor receives police powers to regulate them. This language connects agricultural output with political control: freedom from enslavement and freedom to leave a workplace were not treated as identical questions. The rules are evidence of a governing project, not proof that workers consented or received what was promised.

sections.title: Independence created another political settlement
sections.text: The French expedition of 1802 renewed the threat to emancipation and met resistance. Independence was proclaimed in 1804. The Acte records assembled generals renouncing France; its claim of agreement concerns that gathering. Armitage and Gaffield distinguish the official printed pamphlet and broadside from a lost manuscript stage. They also identify an accompanying oath making Dessalines governor general for life. Political separation and the defense of liberty therefore came with a new concentration of authority. Other records are needed for landholding, work and participation beyond the leaders’ declarations.

returnPrompt: Why is the history of freedom longer than the date of one declaration?

deeperReading.title: A signature, a scribe and a printed name do different work
deeperReading.text: The Smithsonian distinguishes the unidentified writer of the 1797 letter from Louverture’s signature. Its volunteer transcription contains uncertain readings, so the account paraphrases clear passages rather than claiming a complete critical translation. The museum’s brief independence-threat caption is not adopted as this letter’s verified wording. The 1804 document is a different object history: scholarship describes government printing, transmission and authorization. A name reproduced in print is not an autograph, and a printed proclamation is not a verbatim transcript of every speech at Gonaïves.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 18–20: manuscript stage and authorization

deeperReading.title: A constitution supplies a project, not a complete outcome
deeperReading.text: Reading abolition beside cultivation rules exposes a concrete tension. The 1801 text promises a revenue share while restricting movement and assigning the governor enforcement powers. It does not supply each worker’s income, complaint, negotiation or response. Calling the estate a family is a governing metaphor, not evidence of kinship or voluntary agreement. Manigat’s regional account likewise warns against making one group’s situation stand for the whole colony. A fuller investigation needs cultivators’ and women’s accounts, local enforcement records and household evidence. Independence in 1804 did not make those questions disappear; this packet does not extend them into unverified 1825 financial claims.

deeperReading.title: Read political changes forward through time
deeperReading.text: Read the 1797 letter beside article 1 of the 1801 constitution and the 1804 oath. These records first join freedom with French allegiance, then mark a political separation. They do not establish one unchanging intention for every participant. Explaining that change requires the circumstances of each record, rather than assigning the final outcome backward to 1791.

evidenceReading.title: Political voices, work rules and a circulated act
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of French transcriptions and selected scholarship. They are not new critical translations, unmediated access to every enslaved voice or a collation of the original 1804 pamphlet.

items.label: A leader’s letter is an argument to a recipient
items.text: The 1797 Vincent letter seeks advocacy with the French Directory, contests racist allegations and affirms attachment to France.
items.interpretation: It supplies a particular political position at that date. It is not the later Directory letter, a universal statement of formerly enslaved people’s views or evidence that independence was every insurgent’s fixed objective in 1791.

items.label: An abolition clause coexists with work regulation
items.text: Article 3 of the 1801 constitution prohibits slavery; articles 14–16 protect continuing cultivation and empower regulation of cultivators’ movement.
items.interpretation: The combination reveals a governing project and a tension within freedom. It does not establish consent, actual payments or identical enforcement on every estate.

items.label: The act’s recorded agreement has a defined group
items.text: The modern French transcription identifies assembled generals as swearing the 1804 independence oath. Scholarship separately describes the official printed packet.
items.interpretation: Recorded unanimity in that assembly does not establish a population-wide vote. The printed version, manuscript copies, modern transcription and lost manuscript stage must not be treated as one physical object.

familyActivity.title: Separate a right, a work rule and a political decision
steps: Read the supplied capsule together. Make three cards: legal status, control of work and political separation.
Match the 1801 abolition clause, the cultivation/movement rules and the 1804 generals’ oath to the cards. Explain why two cards can describe the same constitution.
Name the group whose agreement the 1804 text records. What source would you seek before claiming that every cultivator agreed or received a promised share?
Write one supported statement and one remaining question. Do not invent a worker’s biography, wage or reply.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: The 1801 constitution prohibits slavery and describes people as free and French. Other articles insist on agricultural work, describe cultivators as sharing revenues and give the governor police authority over movement. The Acte dated 1 January 1804 records assembled generals renouncing France. These are paraphrases of French texts in modern transcriptions. A rule is not evidence that every worker received a share or agreed; the generals’ recorded agreement is not a population-wide vote. The task is answerable from this supplied text; no absent image or historical role-play is required. A household question needs a relevant account or record beyond the formal provisions.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian or Haitian/community acceptance
review.scope: Regional action, shifting emancipation, a named formerly enslaved leader’s mediated letter, constitutional work rules and the authority of an independence act. Six new selected records and one retained-and-renewed source scope. The 4 November review checked Dessalines’s dateline in the digitized official pamphlet, printed p. 7. No new map, media, image, route or historical relation.
limitations: At the October review the Columbia and TNA catalogue pages could not be reopened. On 4 November the closing dateline and printed name on p. 7 were checked directly against the digitized official pamphlet. This inspection covers one printed page. Image reproduction permission remains unresolved.

The 1801 and 1804 French sources are modern transcriptions with listed editions, not original printings independently collated here. English prose is editorial paraphrase, not a critical or adopted published translation. The letter uses volunteer transcription with uncertain readings; no complete original-image collation.

Only Manigat’s printed pp. 363–365 and the specified author-manuscript passages were consulted. Linked bibliography, full edited volume and later 1825 recognition/debt sources were not read or silently adopted.

The northern 1793 proclamation date differs between the compressed English Heritage overview and the parliamentary account. The exact 29 August date is attributed to the latter; provincial measures and the 1794 decree remain separate.

Formerly enslaved actors had different aims and situations. A leader’s letter, an assembly’s oath and official work rules do not recover every cultivator’s voice, women’s experience, actual income, household outcome or universal consent.

No existing dossier image is present and no new asset is supplied. Earlier TNA reproduction-clearance questions remain unresolved; a public-domain statement on the separate Smithsonian letter does not clear TNA images.

Independent historical/Haitian/community review, family usability, screen-reader/physical-device behavior and physical print remain open. Bot source consultation and leaf checks are not those acceptance tasks.
